title: EM in Mixture-of-Experts vs. Dense Models at Matched Parameter Counts

original_idea.problem: A controlled comparison between MoE and dense models for EM is needed to isolate the causal mechanism (sparsity, expert specialization, or parameter count).
original_idea.direction: Use a small MoE model and a parameter-matched dense model. Fine-tune both on identical insecure-code datasets. Evaluate EM rates.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Plausible chain: if sparsity suppresses EM, MoE architectures may offer an architectural safety property. However, the gap is that even if the correlation is confirmed, the mechanism (sparsity vs. expert specialization) is not fully isolated by this experiment alone.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Finding parameter-matched MoE and dense models at small scale is non-trivial. MoE fine-tuning may require specialized configurations. The idea acknowledges this difficulty ('If an MoE model is not readily available... simulate sparse gating'). Simulating sparse gating is an advanced technique beyond beginner level.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Conceptually two fine-tuning runs, but model selection and configuration matching adds substantial setup work. Finding appropriate matched models is a prerequisite that may take significant time. The fallback (simulated sparse gating) expands scope.

novelty.reasoning: 'Emergent Misalignment in Mixture-of-Experts Models' (Doan et al., OpenReview 2025) directly addresses this question. The paper fine-tunes MoE models of different sparsities (GPT-oss-20B, Qwen3-30B-A3B, Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct-v0.1) on insecure code and unsafe medical advice, finding that EM is present in MoE models with few experts but disappears as the number of experts increases — identifying sparsity as a containment mechanism. The negative correlation between sparsity and EM is the exact finding this proposal seeks. The causal mechanism (sparsity vs expert specialization) is directly investigated.
